title: Family of man killed by police want closure
subtitle: Rally to push for inquest date, 3 years after Beau Baker shot
article: Three years ago today, Beau Baker, 20, was shot and killed by a Waterloo Regional Police officer.
Baker's family is still waiting for answers on exactly what happened that night.
"It's been three years," Baker's mother, Jackie Baker, said in an interview. "I'd like for myself and my family to grieve and to heal from this."
Beau, who had mental health issues, was shot after reportedly advancing on police with a knife outside his apartment on Brybeck Crescent in Kitchener.
His mother said it's difficult to grieve when she doesn't know all of the details.
"I haven't been able to say goodbye to Beau yet," she said.
"It's just been very difficult. I need to hear everything."
Ontario's deputy chief coroner announced in October 2016 that an inquest will be held but a date has not been set.
Family and friends of Baker will rally in front of the courthouse on Frederick Street on Tuesday at 12 noon to demand a date be set immediately.
The officer who shot Baker has not been named. Baker's mother hopes the officer will testify at the inquest.
"I want to know who killed my son. I do have to at some point forgive this person."
The lawyer for the Baker family, Davin Charney, sent a letter on Thursday to Ontario's chief coroner.
"The truth of what happened the night that Beau was killed remains unknown to his family and the community," he wrote.
"This delay is agonizing and causes the family to suffer further grief and anxiety."
The family has the right to know the truth, Charney said in an interview.
"We don't know what happened," he said.
"We don't know the name of the officer who did the shooting and other key details about the case.
"What was Beau doing when he was shot and did he have a knife and did he move forward or was he standing still? All those details are essentially being kept secret."
A long delay in holding an inquest undermines it, Charney said, "because people forget or they move or they die. The longer you wait, the less value there is to the process."
Charney said inquests are regularly held years later.
An inquest looking into a fatal shooting by Durham Regional Police happened five years after the death, he said.
"In the U.S., if there's a fatal police shooting, the next day they're releasing in-car cameras or video from bystanders," he said.
"And here it's a coverup for years and years until maybe nobody cares anymore.
"It seems like in Canada we're just way behind in terms of the public having access to information about these things and I really think that entirely protects the police."
